claims.text: Changes in constituent count induce variations in short-range chemical order in single-phase Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni FCC alloys and their quaternary and ternary subsets.
Short-range chemical order modulates the effective stacking-fault energy.
Changes in effective stacking-fault energy govern dislocation mechanisms and mechanical properties including yield strength, strain hardening, and ductility.
The equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy and the investigated quaternary and ternary subsets can be produced as single-phase FCC materials by identical thermomechanical processing.
APT and high-resolution TEM can quantify nanoscale short-range chemical order in these alloys.
Identical processing, including homogenization near 1200°C followed by cold rolling and annealing or solution treatment with controlled cooling, will ensure single-phase FCC microstructures.
Performing room-temperature tests at moderate strain rates under identical processing conditions will ensure that only composition influences the results.
Variations in short-range chemical order alter local bonding and electronic structure.
Changes in local bonding and electronic structure shift the effective stacking-fault energy.
Cost-reduced quaternary and ternary alloys may have lower short-range order than the equiatomic quinary alloy.
Lower short-range order in quaternary or ternary alloys may produce higher or more spatially uniform stacking-fault energy.
Higher stacking-fault energy favors full-dislocation glide over deformation twinning.
Greater short-range order in the equiatomic quinary alloy could locally reduce stacking-fault energy.
Localized stacking-fault-energy reduction could enhance deformation twinning or impede dislocation mobility.
The proposed atomic-scale effects cause differences in yield strength, work hardening, and ductility.
Relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline, alloys with altered, typically reduced, short-range order will exhibit measurable shifts in stacking-fault energy.
Quaternary or ternary alloys with higher stacking-fault energy will favor dislocation glide and exhibit lower strain hardening.
Alloys with lower stacking-fault energy may exhibit more deformation twinning.
Short-range-order metrics, stacking-fault-energy values, and mechanical properties or failure modes will be correlated across the alloy set.

The proposed relationship is limited to single-phase FCC alloys with controlled processing histories tested at room temperature and moderate strain rates, and may not apply to multiphase materials, extreme temperatures, or high strain rates.
